Is it the serious intention of the Government to go on with this Bill this session? It is a very lengthy
and important Bill; there are over 100 amendments in it as well as some new sections; in fact, the railway law of Canada is to be entirely overhauled. From my knowledge of railway legislation, I think it would take this House a. month to handle this Bill, if we gave it the attention it ought to have.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is a good deal of force in what the hon. gentleman says as [DOT] to the importance of the Bill and the necessity for careful and perhaps lengthy consideration. We would like to have the Bill passed this session, but we do not propose to make any attempt to force it through without due consideration and full deliberation. In any event, there is no harm in having the committee appointed and doing what can be done this session in that regard. .
In what position will the committee of the House of Commons be to examine this Bill, unless the Minister of Railways introduces the Bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

On section 1-incorporation; name:

Would some person in
charge of this Bill explain what its purpose is?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not very familiar
with the Bill. I was just looking over it. Sir Edmund Osier, in whose name the Bill stands, is absent through indisposition. There has been an institution in Canada, as my hon. friend knows, called the National Council of Women, which, as I understand, is designed to bring into co-operation various societies and associations of women throughout Canada for charitable, .benevolent and other purposes of a like character. I understand that the object of the Bill is merely to give a more efficient organization by the acquisition of corporate powers. I have looked over the Bill and it does not seem to contain anything of an objectionable character. Perhaps we can take it up clause by clause and have it read.
On section 5-constitution and standing orders:
What does the Premier think of clause 5, by which we legalize the by-laws of the Council, although we know nothing about 'their by-laws?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not familiar with the by-laws of the various local councils; but, inasmuch as the ladies in the various cities and towns of Canada carry on the affairs of these local councils under these by-laws and have done pretty good work,
I think we may safely assume that the by-laws are reasonable, and that if they are not reasonable they will be amended under the provisions of this Act.
Is this the inauguration of female suffrage?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not prepared to answer that, because I really do not know anything more about the Bill than my hon. friend; and, in the absence of Sir Edmund Osier, I thought I would like to help it along if I could.

The House in committee on Bill 143, respecting a patent of John Arnoldi.-Mr. Macdonell. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-power to commissioner of patents for extension of patent:
What is this patent?

This is a patent against whose renewal our department raise no objection. Arnoldi, the patentee, had paid in fees for two terms, that is twelve years, and then became very ill just before the final payment was due, so that he could not attend to his own business and would not allow anyone else to do so, and the third payment lapsed. The patent is the only thing left to the widow, who is the beneficiary legatee, and she asks that she may be allowed to revive it through this Bill. The Senate unanimously passed it, and our department raise no objection under the circumstances.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speechtext:
The House in committee on Bill 142, respecting the Trans-Canada and Hudson Bay Railway Company.-Mr. Douglas. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-extension of time:

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I was unable, on account of the state of my health, to be here on Friday night, but I understand from leading 'Hansard' that some hon. gentlemen desired an explanation of this Bill. We have passed the Bill from the Senate as printed without any amendment. It iB the first extension of time asked for this line of railway, and, of course, to that extent the Railway Committee had some sympathy with it. It originated in 1912. The line runs from Edmonton to Port Nelson or Fort Churchill, and from Lone river to Peace river, crossing thence

through Laurier pass to Prince Rupert or Portland canal. It is about a thousand miles in length, and the capitalization in 1912 was fixed at $10,000,000.

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Who are the promoters?

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I have not the original act of incorporation before me, so I cannot give that information. The only objection made in the committee was as to the name. One hon. gentleman thought that the words Hudson bay were objectionable, but he did not press the objection. The difficulty is that the company has had corporate powers since 1912 by the Act of this Parliament, and in the absence of some very good reason for making a change in name we did not like to make one.

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
What is the route of the railway from Edmonton? I am informed the route is through Athabaska Landing. If so, I shall be glad to consent to the extension of time, but if it is not routed through Athabaska Landing, I want it so routed as a condition of the extension of time.
M<r. LANCASTER: As a matter of fact, I cannot say that it is, or is not so routed. The language is not so specific as that. It reads: 'from Edmonton to Port Nelson '' and the railway is not required to run actually though Athabaska Landing. The Minister of Railway will have to deal with that question in approving the route map.

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I wish to make very emphatic objection to the extension of time in the charter. Either the charter means nothing at all, or it means that .a railway will be built. If it means nothing at all, it should not encumber the statute book. There are certain railroads built, and building, to the northwest and to the northeast of Edmonton. If this railroad is to be routed approximately near Athabaska Landing, as the representative of that district, I want it routed through Athabaska Landing. I do not want this railroad to be able to hold up an established town that is adjacent to their proposed line of railway. If, on the contrary, it is routed to pass a considerable distance from Athabaska Landing I have nothing to complain of; but as the representative of that district I want to know what is the intention of Parliament in this matter, .and to have the interests of this established town protected so faT as Parliament can protect them.

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I see that the section does make it an alternative.

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I notice that the original Bill provides that the company may build from a point at or near the city of Edmonton, thence northerly by the most feasible route to, at, or near Athabaska Landing.
I do not object to the words ' at or near ' in the case of Edmonton, which is an established city and railroad centre, and a railway constructed thereabouts would necessarily be constructed from Edmonton. The interests of the railroad would compel that, but in the case of Athabaska Landing the position is different, and I would like the committee to amend the charter in order to make the railway run through Athabaska Landing.

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Perhaps we can do
that here. If the House is unanimous, we could strike out the words ' at or near.'

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That would be very satisfactory to me.

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Then I would move
that a new section be added at the end of the Bill as follows:
Section 8 of chapter 134 of the statutes of 1912 is amended by striking out the words ' at, or near ' after the word ' to ' in the fifth line of the said section.

maintopic: PACIFIC, TRANS-CANADA AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member had better give notice of that amendment; then it will not be necessary for him to be here when the Bill goes through.
Progress reported.

The House again in Committee on Bill No. 141, respecting Rainy River Radial Railway Company.-Mr. Carrick. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

This Bill, which
came to us from the Senate, has not been amended at all except that we added the standard clause, which prevents the con-
struction on highways without the consent of municipalities.

This is a renewal of a charter granted in 1910. One of the questions that arise frequently in connection with the renewal of charters is in reference to the distribution of electric energy and the powers in connection with it. The Railway Committee has adopted a standard clause, and inserts it even in a renewal of a charter. Has that been done in this case ?

There are three
standard clauses that we now insert in every railway charter. One is as to water-powers and electricity, one as to putting up poles upon the highways, and the other as to securing the authority of the municipality before constructing upon highways. The first two are in the charter as passed in 1910, and the third is inserted by our amendment.
What is the route of this railway ?
I suppose the reason for getting a charter in this Parliament was that the fact that it touches the Minnesota border makes it an international railway. Is this an electric railway ?
I do not think so.
Is it intended to get the water-power from Rainy river ? There are a good many water-powers on Rainy river and these are in dispute between Minnesota and Ontario.

This charter seems to raise a very serious question, and I think the acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) should state the position of the Government with regard to it. It will be noticed

that this railway touches the United States boundary at two points. I am sure the House would like to know, and know very definitely, whether it is the intention of the Government, in sanctioning this charter, to permit the carriage of wheat from the Canadian West into the United States. Surely, there are enough railways now crossing the boundary diverting the trade of Canada to the United States and preventing profit-earnings upon Canadian transcontinental lines without any more such railways being permitted. We would like to have a declaration from the Minister of Railways upon that point.

This Bill came up in the
Railway Committee the other day. I was not present, having another committee to attend. I have not looked into the matter very carefully and would not like to pass an opinion now. If there are any objections or if the question is deemed important, we will let the Bill stand over. But I am surprised to hear the hon. member objecting to more railways taking wheat into the United States, because he was urging that very strongly a day or two ago.

That will not do. I am not objecting to the Bill; I am asking for a declaration of principle in regard to the Bill by the Government whose policy is distinctly against the carrying of wheat into the United States as that policy was put forward by the Minister of Finance in his Budget speech, and I think by almost every other hon. member on that side who followed him.
I think that was the policy of the hon. member when the Transcontinental Bill was brought in-that is, to bring wheat from the West through Canada. I hope he has not changed his policy.

Of course, if it is necessary to explain, the explanation is that the policy of those who established the Transcontinental was to provide all facilities foa-the export of the productions of the West in every available direction-whether by the construction of the Transcontinental, the construction of the Hudson Bay railway or the construction of lines across the international boundary. It was hon. gentlemen opposite who opposed the construction of lines across the international boundary. Yet, though in control of the House, they sanction the building of such lines.
As a matter of fact, on that point the Government is not serious; that is the explanation.
Oh, oh.

They are just talking for effect, and not for traffic. This Act was passed in 1910, and consequently it must be a fairly good Act. What I wranted to get at was just where the railway ran and what its powers were. I had the route generally in mind, but wished to know it more definitely. So far as the traffic north and south is concerned, the increase in traffic between Canada and the United States shows the wisdom of improving facilities for that traffic. For, so long as that traffic is profitable, you cannot stop it. I think that after the explanation of the promoter of the Bill we ought to let it pass, as the Government now say it is their policy to have all the railroads possible.
Is the expression ' at or near ' Rainy river all right ?

I think that is satisfactory.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

The House in Committee on Bill No. 97, to incorporate the All Red Line Railway Company (its title to be the Labrador, Quebec and Southern Railway Company).- Mr. Fripp. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-incorporation:

There is an amendment to section 1 as to the name, striking out the words ' All Red Line ' and inserting the words 'Labrador, Quebec and Southern.' The Bill was very much cut down in the Railway Committee. The company were seeking powers to build from Labrador to the Pacific ocean. They found they could not get such a Bill through, and concluded they would go from Labrador to Quebec only. That makes it a reasonable charter, and we cut down the mileage, the capitalization and the bonding powers to suit.

Who are the promoters
of the line of railway?

The promoters'names are given in section 1 of the Bill, as follows-

Edward J. Holland, agent, of the town of Prescott, in the province of Ontario; Freeman H. Palmer, manufacturer, and Walter F. Stafford, manufacturer, both of the city of Buffalo, in the state of New York, one of the United States; George F. Hope, agent, and George A. White, agent, both of the city of Toronto.

That really originates
in Prescott.
I will not acknowledge that.
Two in Toronto, two in Buffalo, and one in Prescott.

The acting Minister of Railways will have to take a good deal of responsibility for this Bill, as it really originates in his own town. It seems reasonable that this railway project would not be launched without consultation with him.
This is not the project that was originally launched.
The minister opposed the project that was launched; this is it as we cut it down.

This is the remnant, and no doubt the hon. gentleman will 'be responsible for it. Can the acting minister tell us what backing there is behind the project and what was in the mind of the promoters when they proposed the original charter? It may be of deep interest to the people of the country to know what the promoters originally wanted, and why it was curtailed. Why were they not allowed to carry on their philanthropic intention to the full? No doubt the acting Minister of Railways knows all that, seeing that the principal promoter is a neighbour of his.
Mr. F. A. Knapp of Prescott was the only one who spoke to me about the original proposal of a railway from Labrador to the Pacific coast.

Is that the Knapp of
Knapp's roller boat?

Yes. Mr. Holland, who is
mentioned among the promoters, is Mr. Knapp's son-in-law. Mr. Knapp asked me simply if I would urge that the Bill go through; but, instead of doing that, I opposed it very very strongly, for ' the reason that I did not think any one could get sufficient backing to build a railway from Labrador to the Pacific coast.

What do you think about it now?
[Mr. Lancaster 1

I think now as I thought then, that he could not get sufficient backing to build a railway from Labrador to the Pacific coast, and I opposed the Bill. It came before the Railway Committee, but I was attending a meeting of the Redistribution Committee and could not be present. He tells me now that he 4 p.m. has sufficient backing to build the road from the Labrador coast to Quebec, and he said he had Mr. Gould of New York and several other capitalists interested in it.
Is that the Mr. Gould who is building a railway in New Brunswick?

I have not the slightest idea. I would not feel justified in allowing a railway Bill to go through, for what is called the All Red line, from Labrador to the Pacific coast, because I believed it would be simply a promoter's scheme, and for that reason I opposed it. But the committee felt they were justified in reducing it to a railway from Labrador to Quebec.
The minister is right in saying that they should not be allowed to call it the All Red line. My own opinion is that it will never be any more than a thin red line on the map.
That is what I think myself.

And 1 am not quite so sure that it is a proper thing to charter them to build a railway from Labrador to Quebec. The acting minister tells us he was at the Redistribution Committee instead of being at the Railway Committee, but so far as I am concerned I think he would do far better work in the Railway Committee, in the interests of the country at large. I am not satisfied with what he is doing in the Redistribution Committee, and I am only partially satisfied with what he is doing in the Railway Committee.
I have done nothing in tlie Redistribution Committee yet.

I am afraid your intentions are bad. We have been in the habit here, of, in almost every instance, giving charters for railways in the hope that something would come of it, but we are rapidly arriving at a point where we can afford to be more careful about giving indiscriminate charters, else we may stop some legitimate project, which would have substantial backing. I do not know enough about this charter to oppose it, but I do

believe it is proper to curtail its powers and to prevent these people calling it the All Red line, which might deceive investors in the old land, and we do not want any more of that.

Is it alleged by the promoters that they have made any arrangement for steamships to connect with this railway from a Labrador port? Has the minister considered as to the right of this Parliament to grant a charter in territory which is now in dispute with Newfoundland? Where do the promoters expect to get the capital for this enterprise?

The only information I have as to the financial backing of the road is that Mr. F. A. Knapp of the town of Prescott gave me his word that Mr. Gould of New York and other wealthy men were interested in it.
Which Mr. Gould?

He simply said, Mr. Gould of New York. So far as I am concerned, I must say that I have not sufficient evidence before me to justify me in saying to the House that I believe there is sufficient financial backing to build this railroad. As to the right to go through Labrador, as I understand it, this Bill only grants a charter to the Labrador boundary line. I do not kno-w anything about their arranging for steamships. No doubt the promoters will try to float the scheme, but I do not myself believe that this road will be built for some time.
It was stated in the Railway Committee that the promoters of this Bill had already received a charter from Newfoundland, for steamships to the Labrador coast.

I wish again to draw the attention of the House to the change of policy on the part of the Government aB regards railways. Within the last quarter of an hour we have seen the acting Minister of Railways support and pilot through the House a charter to build a railway to the international boundary at two points, and now we hear him avow his opposition to the project of a railway running east and west, intended quite evidently to carry the products of the western plains to the European markets by the most available railroad route. I would like to know if this is a reversal of policy, merely on the part of the Department of Railways under the acting minister, or, if it is to be taken by the country as a new departure by the Government at large. This, it would appear to me, would be a very appropriate time for the House to be informed exactly as to where the Government stands on this very important question of railroad construction, east and west, and north and south.

I would not object to a charter being granted for the building of a railroad from Labrador to the Pacific coast, if I thought there would be any possibility of the promoters building it.
On the Other hand, when a promoter comes before the Railway Committee with a Bill to incorporate the All Red Line Railway Company, which in my opinion may result in a scheme being floated which, I believe, will be only a promoter's scheme after all,
I feel perfectly justified in preventing that Bill from going through, in the interest of those who might subscribe for stock and also in the interest of the good name of Canada. It would not matter to me whether the line were east and west or north and south. I opposed this Bill simply for the reason that I believe it was a scheme that, if allowed to go through, might result in a great loss to those who might subscribe, and injure the good name of Canada in raising money in other countries.

I am sure the House will congratulate the Government upon the new policy now enunciated by the acting Minister of Railways, namely, that the Government will assume responsibility for the bona fides of railroad charters put through this House. There is no doubt that, if that were done, it would have a very beneficial effect upon railroad construction in Canada. From what the minister has said, I presume we are bound to conclude that the large number of charters- which have been put through this session have been examined by the Department of Railways, that the fact of their having gone through with Government sanction is -an assurance of the bona fides of the applicants, and that we may be assured that these Taikoads will be constructed.

On this measure a situation has developed that should be considered by the House. We are building a railway to Hudson bay, and I assume that the Minister of Railways will very shortly ask this House to vote large appropriations in connection with the terminals on the bay. This Tailway will bring into active communication with the rest of 'Canada the

whole of the coast from Hudson bay to the strait of Belle Isle. I noticed, not long ago the statement with reference to the visit to England of Sir Edward Morris that one of his chief objects in going there was to settle the question as to whether Canada or Newfoundland had the absolute right to the territory along the coast. The title and the right of government to that territory will become of vital importance to Canada with the construction of the Hudson Bay railway; and the proposal in this Bill that we should give the right to construct a railway from a point in the province of Quebec to a Labrador port, and the statement made that this company has obtained from the Newfoundland Government chartered rights over this disputed territory, brings acutely before the House the question where this Government stands in regard to this point. On the map of the Dominion of Canada there is a yellow tinge along the coast from the strait of Belle Isle north, and it has always Ibeen assumed that that was the territory over which Newfoundland claimed to have some control. I would regard it as unfortunate if the Dominion of Canada did not control every atom of territory from the Atlantic to the Pacific. In view of the development of Hudson bay this question of control becomes exceedingly important. Would the Prime Minister tell us what is the situation in regard to the disputed territory?

I do not see how the building of the Hudson Bay railway comes into the question, because the terminus will be at Port Nelson. Labrador runs from the strait of Belle Isle to the head of the Hudson strait. I do not think it goes around the whole bay to Port Nelson. The proposed railway is to go west near the strait of Belle Isle from a place called Cape St. Charles, which, I think, is only 50 or 100 miles from the strait, so that there will not be raised any question between Labrador and Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Some difficulty arose about the exact form of question which should be submitted for the determination of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. It was found that under an Imperial statute this question could be decided by the Judicial Committee itself.

As a matter of law
or as a matter of arbitration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Judicial Committee would act under the provisions of an Imperial statute.

As a matter of
law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would have to be a matter of law. I do not know the exact provisions of the statute at this moment. The matter has been altogether in the hands of the Department of Justice, and I am not very familiar with it except as to these particulars. There was a distinct agreement between the two Governments that the matter should be referred to the Judicial Committee; but when it came to settling the form of the question to be submitted, a difference of opinion arose, and I understood that, under an Imperial statute, it was competent for the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council to settle the form, and proceedings were taken for that purpose.

I know something about this matter, because a question arose some years ago with respect to it. The Newfoundland Government gave a license to cut timber upon the Labrador coast. The Quebec Government had also given a license. The holders of the license from the Quebec Government and the holders of the license from the Newfoundland Government found their rights clashing, and the matter was referred to the late Government of the Dominion. The suggestion was made to refer the matter to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. So the matter stood when the late Government left' office. I do not know what has happened since; perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) will inform the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that action was taken between the parties in the dispute referred to. Representations were

made to the Government by the Government of the province of Quebec and upon those representations being communicated to the Home Government it was suggested that the question of the boundaries between Labrador and Newfoundland should be referred to the Privy Council under a statute of William IV which makes provision for such a reference. Or rather, the original representation made to the Home Government was in the form of a complaint that Newfoundland had been infringing upon our territory. The Home authorities communicated with the Newfoundland Government who answered that they were within their lines and within their rights in what they had done. Thereupon, the Home Government suggested that there should be a reference to the Privy Council and also that the Newfoundland Government and the Government of Canada should agree upon such a reference. This was agreed to and there followed negotiations looking to a settlement of the precise form of the proceedings that should be taken in the matter. Furthermore, the province of Quebec, being directly interested, represented that they ought to be parties to the case. So far as that representation is concerned, we felt that the issue being with an outside possession the Dominion was the proper party to act, but we did agree that in applying to the Privy Council we should act in consultation with them, and if they desired to name counsel in connection with the drawing of the pleadings we would be agreeable. Then,	if they	thought
proper to ask the Privy Council that they should be represented	at the
hearing we would make no objection. Upon that matter being so adjusted, with the co-operation of the provincial government, ot at all events counsel named by them, the next step was to arrange with the Government of Newfoundland as to the proceedings to be followed. In reference to that, interviews were held in London last summer, and we were under the impression that final agreement had been arrived at. It would appear, however, that, as I presume, when the matter was reported to the Newfoundland authorities, they took exception to the form in which the question was put. Thereupon, as it seemed to us, that the question as agreed to was properly put, and agreement being apparently impossible, we approached the British Government and asked that the question should 'be by His Majesty referred generally to their Lordships under the statute of William IV. to which I have referred, leaving it to them
finally to fix the precise form in which the question should be submitted to them, and also the proceedings to be taken. And the matter stands in that position.

The wording of this Bill recognizes the existence of a boundary line between the territory of Canada and the territory of Labrador. If hon. members will refer to section 8 they will see that that is so. In view of the situation in which this matter stands between Canada and Newfoundland, is it wise for us to pass legislation in this House which plainly recognizes the existence of a boundary, whereas we are proposing to argue before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council that no such boundary exists. _

So far as the Bill is
concerned, I was going to say that the question which the hon. member has raised is one of great importance, and so I would ask that the committee allow the Bill to stand until another day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not understand that we propose to argue that there is no boundary line; on the contrary we contend that the precise points through which that Line is to be drawn are fixed by the proclamation that dealt with the matter, and what we propose to 'have referred for determination was just where this line runs as a matter of fact and what land lies on one side of the boundary and what lies on the other. My recollection is that the instrument gives Newfoundland that part of the Labrador coast that lies eastward of a line drawn from a certain point direct north to a certain parallel. What we hope for under this adjudication is to learn just where that line runs on the land itself. We do not say there is no boundary, but we say that it is necessary to determine in accordance with what is defined, just where the line so defined, runs.

I apprehended-oi
course, I may be incorrect-that the question was how much of this northern land was under the protectorate of the Colony of Newfoundland for the purpose of maintaining order, etc. I was not aware tlhat there was any defined territory there constituting a part of Newfoundland. It would seem to me desirable-and I have no doubt the minister is already seized of this point-that Canada should, if possible, establish territorial rights to every part of the land that is within what is known as the Dominion of Canada in a territorial sense. While Newfoundland may, on account of her situation

and proximity, foe the Government in the 'best position to deal with it so far as protectorate is concerned, yet Canada, having acquired larger responsibility in the northern country which slhe is now exploiting, should obtain control-by negotiation or otherwise-absolute control, of the territory there. This question is important, and I think well worthy of consideration in connection with the terms of this Bill. We should not pass legislation which could and might he urged as having some effect in fixing the boundary line.

May I be permitted on
this item to draw the attention of the minister to the St. Peter's canal in Richmond county, Nova Scotia. For the last two years the department has had under construction very considerable improvements at the St. Peter's canal, and for some reason, which is attributed to a necessary change to be made in the location of the lock, that work has been suspended for some time. From information I have received from various sources, I understand that this change involves a considerable increase in the original contemplated outlay. It is very important that as little delay as possible should take place in the carrying on of this work. It is an important waterway which opens up the Bras D Or lake for navigation to coasting vessels. For the past two years work has been carried on, and a great many labouring men have obtained employment there. I ask the minister to take the earliest steps possible to make arrangements, either with the present contractor or by calling for new tenders, if that be necessary, so that the work may be continued. I understand that the present plan of the department necessitates the closing of the canal for a season, and if that be so it is of the utmost importance that notice be given immediately to all parties interested in the navigation of the Bras d'Or lake. It is also desirable that the canal should toe
5 p.m. closed as early as possible, so that one season only shall be lost. Would the minister make a statement to the committee as to the present position of the work on the St. Peter s canal?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. D. REID (Acting Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
The memorandum I have before me, with reference to the work on the St. Peter's canal, states: That this work is under contract to a Mr. W. H. Weller; that owing to the extremely hard nature of the material to be excavated, necessitating drilling and blasting before it can be removed, coupled with the very bad weather encountered last season, this work is very much behind, and instead of being completed on November 30, 1913, as called for, it will, from present indications, not be completed until some time in 1915. The matter has been before me several times. The representative of the contractor has been urging that some new arrangement shall be made, for the reason that the material they found, as they proceeded with the work, is very much harder, and is different from that set out in the specifica-

tions. Mr. Bowden, the chief engineer, feels that it would be better for us to get a new site for the lock. If this were done, St. Peter's canal would be closed all this season. Mr. Bowden tells me that if we allow the present contractors to take a new site and proceed with the work at the present prices, it can be gone on with at once. He tells me further, that it will cost probably $100,000 more to build this new lock, and I have hesitated up to the present. I must, however, take the matter up within the next few days, as I am exceedingly anxious to have the work commence immediately. I was unable to decide upon the matter before, as I have been very busy recently. I think I will feel justified in recommending to Council that the suggestion of Mr. Bowden to erect a new lock and close the canal during its construction might be considered. I was very much afraid, however, that if we did that we would be censured for closing the canal for the whole season. As I understand from the remarks just made by the hon. member (Mr. Kyte), if the work is proceeded with now and the canal closed for the season, he thinks that would be the least objectionable course to the people interested. I am giving the matter my serious consideration. I discussed it with the chief engineer to-day, and I hope to arrive at some conclusion within a few days. I will be able to give the hon. member more definite information before my Estimates are finally passed.

I am quite familiar with the change that seems to be necessary, owing to what has developed, as the work progressed. It was originally intended to construct the lock in the new portion of the canal. That was found to be impossible owing to the failure to locate, rock bottom at the place where the new lock was to be located, and it necessitated the placing of the new lock in an oblique position across the present canal. That rendered it necessary to close the canal for a longer period than was originally intended. As there is no way of avoiding that difficulty, however, .and inasmuch as it will be necessary to close the canal to traffic, I think the best judgment would be that the earlier it is closed the earliar it will be reopened for traffic.	a
Another point I wish to impress upon the minister is that for the past two years a considerable amount of employment has been given to the labouring people in that
[Mr. J. D. Reid.l
part of the country. Employment is not as readily obtainable at the present time in that portion of Nova Scotia as it formerly was, and a great many people will be very much disappointed if the work is delayed for any considerable time. A number of these people had theretofore pursued the calling of fishermen; but, owing to the guarantees they had of continued work for a few years they gave up their other occupation, and they now find themselves without any employment whatever. For that reason, in addition to those I have already given, I think it is of the greatest importance that the work be continued so that employment may be given to those men who are dependent upon that work for their livelihood during the course of time the work will be in progress.

I realize that it is very important to these men and also to the contractor that they be not kept waiting for the decision .any longer than is possible. I will therefore give this matter almost immediate attention and come to some decision as to what will be done.

I am also particularly
interested in the navigation -of the St. Peter's canal. The county which I have the honour to represent has several industries, the transportation from which depends upon the capacity of that canal. It has been already pointed out by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) that practically the capacity of navigation of the Bras d'Or lakes depends upon the capacity of the St. Peter's canal. There are two other outlets to the sea from the Bras d'Or lakes, but ships going to the sea find it safer and shorter to go through the canal. The other day I had a letter from the president of the Victoria Gypsum Company, a concern doing considerable business on these lakes, making inquiries about the improvements to the canal. At present they are unable to go through the canal; but after the improvements are made, they hope to be able to use it. It would be a great pity if it were necessary to close the navigation of the canal for the whole summer. I do not know much about canal work, but I think much of the work could be done in the winter time, as the frost in that part of the country is not so severe that cement and excavation work cannot be done just as well in winter as in summer. Pumping and such other work as is necessary can also be done in the winter time. I think that the work should be advanced as far as possible in

all its stages before the closing of the canal takes place. There is such a thing as contractors not being sufficiently advanced with their work before they take that step. For instance, the minister will find parties commencing the building of a wharf before they have all their material ready, and in that way dragging along with the work very much longer than necessary. Very slow progress is being made in the work on this canal, and I am afraid that the contractors are not doing all that should be done in order to push forward with vigour this important work; in fact, I understand that nothing at all has been done during the whole of this winter. In our part of the country the winter is the very best time for cutting a canal, for the removal of clay and so on. I hope that the work will be pushed forward as rapidly as possible; and that the minister will take caTe to make the term of the closing of the canal as short as possible, as it will interfere with a great many industries there and with the route of a number of steamers that go to Newfoundland, such as the Seal, a very large steamer, the steamer that carries the French mail from Halifax to St. Pierre, and a number of other boats of a similar kind.

I would like to know from the acting minister if a decision has yet been reached as to whether or not the canal and the Welland river at the town of Welland are to be put on the same level, with a dam at the village of Port Robinson, the river from the town of Welland to the village of Port Robinson being used as a canal. The contracts are being let, and, if the work is to be completed in the time estimated by the chief engineer of the canal and by the chief engineer of the department, I think a decision should be reached forthwith as to that matter.

That question has not come before me at all so far, and this is the first I have heard of any difference of opinion in regard to the matter. If the hon. member will let it stand for a few moments, I have sent for information and shall be glad to take it up again.

I shall be very glad to do so. I supposed that the acting Minister of Railways knew something about the affairs of his department. The present canal is carried over the Welland river by an aqueduct. The proposition of the engineer in charge of the Welland canal is to put a dam in the Welland river four miles below Welland, to raise the level of
the river by five feet and to lov^er the level of the canal by four feet, so as to put them on the same level, thus flooding a large area of land west of the town of Welland and to some extent east of the town. It is a matter that has reached such proportions that it should be attended to immediately.

I am not opposed to the Welland canal; far from it. We are for the Welland canal, but w.e are also for the Georgian Bay canal. Whilst I do not wish to launch into another debate on the Georgian Bay canal, as the matter was brought up not very long ago before the ministers who received the huge delegation from Montreal and from northern Ontario on that subject, yet I regret that the Government has not thought proper, after the very complete investigation which took place some years ago when the late Administration was in office, to undertake the construction of the canal. It is well known, and nobody doubts it, that the answer given the other day by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) means that the Georgian Bay project is shelved for many, many years to come. I am inclined to believe-in fact, I know- that at least one of the three commissioners appointed on that new commission is himself deadly opposed to the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. That is a secret which is now public amongst the businessmen of Montreal.
What does the hon. gentleman say?

I will give the name to my hon. friend if he wants it. I regret that the ministers who represent the district of Montreal are not in their places. I include the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) amongst the three. The people of Montreal, the Board of Trade, the Chambre de Commerce and the Civic Federation have declared on many occasions that the construction of the Georgian Bay canal would be the logical completion of our transportation system. They had hoped that the present Government would favour the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. But it is evident, from what I have heard of late, that the present Government is opposed to its construction, and will stand only by the construction of the Welland canal. I am told that the opposition to the Georgian Bay canal which suddenly came the other day from

the Quebec Board of Trade was engineered so as to show to the public that there was a division of opinion in the province of Quebec as regards that great undertaking. But the minister may be assured that public opinion is unanimous on that question in our province. Now, I would like to get a frank statement from the hon. gentleman:	Does the Government intend, yes or no, to proceed with the work? Or is it intended to deepen the section of the French river in order to give North Bay the whole benefit of the work and leave the other sections unconstructed? To hand over to a new commission the question of the commercial advantages of the project is, to say the least, simply farcical. A commission sat years ago in the Senate and the best experts in the country were heard, amongst them being no less a personage than Sir William Van Horne himself. Much as we may differ with the ' opinions of Sir William Van Horne in polities, especially on reciprocity, yet everybody will admit that on transportation matters he is a great authority indeed. Well, he gave his evidence, and my hon. friend can read it in the report which was published. He will see that the ex-president of the Canadian Pacific railway is not only a friend, but nn advocate, an ardent advocate of the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. Now, why fool the people of Northern Ontario and of the province of Quebec with another commission? Has Mr. Gohier, who was appointed by the Government as one of the commissioners, agreed to sit on that new board? The hon. gentleman can probably give us the information. Before I take my seat, I say again, it is simply fooling the people to pretend favouring the construction of the canal, and at the same time to appoint a new commission, when two commissions have already been appointed, and possibly fifty expensive reports have been published dealing with the subject on its merits and giving all possible data to the Government. I would like to get a straight answer from the hon. gentleman.
The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) gets up at a moment when the ministers from the district of Montreal happen to be away-
They are never here.
They are here most o: the time and oftener than the member for Rouville.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is never here.

He is always here as a matter of fact. But some members of the Government have other public affairs to attend to, and I think it most unfortunate that the suggestion should be thrown across the floor that the members of the Government from one district are away, and that at a moment when we are discussing the Railways and Canals Estimates. The Georgian Bay canal, which does not relate to this department, should not be brought up now. It is under the Public Works Department.
Is it not germane to what is before the committee?

It may or may not be. But the hon. member, in order to gain an advantage as against the members of the Cabinet from the Montreal district, rises to discuss the Georgian Bay canal when the Railway Estimates are under discussion, which is not the proper moment for the consideration of this mattter. It may have something to do with it, but it is not the time when the subject of the Georgian Bay canal is supposed to be taken up. As I say, it is when the Public Works Estimates are under discussion would be the opportune time for the consideration of this matter. But the hon. member, seeing that the members of the Cabinet from the Montreal district are away, and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) is away-because we are not considering his Estimates-takes this as the time to ask for a proper and complete answer from the Government on this Georgian Bay canal proposition. That is, he puts his question at a moment when he knows that the minister who can answer him is not here. My hon. friend has said that the Quebec Board of Trade resolution was ' engineered,' to use his own expression. He has only repeated what was said in the newspapers on this subject. But I wish to take this opportunity of telling the hon. gentleman that the 'members of the council of the Quebec Board of Trade are honourable men, and they have .answered this allegation that the resolution which they passed was ' engineered ' or inspired. Everybody will understand what the statement of the-hon. gentleman means; no names are given. The members of the council of the Board of Trade of Quebec, have over the signature of their president or secretary- president, I think-declared in the most emphatic manner that nothing of the kind

was suggested to them, that nobody approached them and that in this matter they had expressed their own opinion. As a matter of fact, I wish to declare here from my seat in the House that I have not had an interview with any member of the council of the Quebec Board of Trade about this, and, moreover, that what they have expressed does not represent my own views. That is going as far as a man can go, and I hope will once and for all put a stop to the suggestion that the Quebec Board of Trade is being used against this proposition.
What are your views?

My views are that we were face to face with this proposition, which is a very big one, and that we had to inquire into its commercial feasibility. Consequently we have appointed a commission to make a report upon it.
That is to say you have no views at all.
Your views are not established yet.

If I had views about the question as it stands aft present, and if the Government had decided about it, surely there would be no need of a commission. The commission has been appointed in order to have further light on the commercial feasibility of the project. The hon. member for Rouvilfe sayis that we are fooling the people and that one of the commissioners has his mind made up on this project. If that is so, it would be my hon. friend's duty to enlighten the public. He has said1 he would let me know personally, but then I would not be at liberty to make use of the information.

As Montreal is not
represented on the commission, I shall let my hon. friend know.

I shall invite my hon. friend to give the information not in a private manner, but openly in the House, so that the public will know about it. I think that would be the best course to adopt under the circumstances.
Is this commission one of those of which the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke of as consuming good ink and paper but doing nothing for the country, or is it some other kind of a commission!

It may be that in late years commissions of that kind have been
appointed, but this is not that kind. The commission has to its credit and foir its merit the fact that its members are going to work for ithe public and to make this report without being paid for it. They are working in the public interest.

Then the
others were not?

I agree that many of the commissions appointed by my right hon. friend were not, and they were paid money out of the public treasury for doing nothing. Here we have the very reverse : we have a serious commission which is going to do some good work and which is not going to cost the country much. We have appointed this commission, and the fact that the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) says we are trying to fool the people will not cause us to recall the commission. We have acted seriously in appointing the commission; we intend that it shall do its work, and we will wait for its report. My hon. friend is much mew in a hurry about the Georgian Bay canal now than when he was on this side of the House.

That is the old
story.
A very old story, and it is true.

My hon. friend was not in the last Parliament, but we have had three sessions under a new Government. That Government have never done a single thing themselves in reference to anything under heaven about which they did not say when asked any question: You did not do something ten years ago. Can you not get some new argument?

I am sorry if I have said anything that will hurt the feelings of my hon. friend from Piotou, with whom 1 am such good friends, but after all how can we dispose of these questions? The members of the late Government had this question before them for years, and they did not decide anything about it; and now, when we have appointed a commission to inquire into the commercial feasibility of the project, they are in such a hurry that the commission does not count for anything; they want us to come to a decision before we have the report of that commission. If we did that we would be stultifying ourselves; and, in spite of my earnest wish to be agreeable to the hon. member for Rouville, I will tell him that

no decision will be arrived at on the Georgian Bay canal scheme before the commission has reported on it.

I am very glad that the hon. member for Rouville has brought this question before the House. I know that the Georgian Bay canal comes up under the Estimates of the Minister of Public Works, but the whole scheme of the Georgian Bay canal has always been associated with the Welland canal, and it is very seldom that the Welland canal has been under discussion without a word being said about the Georgian Bay canal. I listened with interest to the remarks of the Postmaster General. His views are not exactly the views of the Minister of Public Works, as I understood that minister to speak to the delegation the other day. He did not say to wait until the commission would report before the Government would commit itself. He told the delegation that they would have to wait until the Prime Minister's return when he would lay their request before him. We know that the Prime Minister is back from Virginia, and without doubt the minister has placed the delegation's request before him. The Prime Minister is within the building now, and perhaps could be brought into the House to tell us whether the Georgian Bay canal is going to be built or not. The Postmaster General said this afternoon that as the ministers of the Montreal district were absent the Georgian Bay canal could not possibly be built. There is absolutely no doubt that is what he said.
I am sorry my English is so bad.

The member for Rouville (Mo-. Lemieux) asked that the Government give a serious answer to the question as to whether or not they intended to construct the Georgian Bay canal, and the Postmaster General said that it was unfair for the member for Rouville to bring this question up this afternoon and expect an answer to be given by the Government. Then, remembering that the Ministar of Public Works had .said, ' Wait till the Prime Minister returns from Virginia ' the Postmaster General said: ' This is not fair. The Government cannot give an answer because the ministers for the district of Montreal are not here.'

My hon. friend has no right to put words into my mouth which
[Mr Pelletier.]
I did not use. Perhaps my English is so-bad that-
It is very good.

I said it was not fair of the hon. member for Rouville to bring this question up when the ministers were away. I said that the Georgian Bay canal concerned the Department of the Minister of Public works, and that the question could not be discussed ini his absence. That is fair from meaning what the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) said.

Whether the Minister of Public Works is in his seat or not, the building of the Georgian Bay canal is a national question, not a political one, and it is a question upon which the Government ought to be prepared at all times to give their views. The late Government never hesitated to do so. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, when Pirime Minister, said time and again from his seat in this House that the Georgian Bay canal would be built. Practically every one of his ministers similarly committed themselves from their seats in this House in answer to questions put to them by members on both sides of the House. The hon. member for Rouville explained this afternoon that the delegation that came here a few days ago was not satisfied with, the answer given by the Minister of Public Works, and he asked the Government to give a direct answer to the questions: Is it the intention of the Government to go on with the building of the Georgian Bay canal, or is it their intention not to build the Georgian Bay canal? I have had a seat in this House for nearly ten years and I know what has been done by the late Government in connection with the Georgian Bay canal, and I know, unfortunately, what has not been done by the present Government. The late Government had a most extensive report prepared by the engineers of the Public Works Department. Any one who reads that report will find it most comprehensive; it not only settled the engineering feasibility of the canal, but gave enough information to determine on its commercial feasibility also. We also have the report of the special committee .appointed by the Senate a few years ago, which contains testimony from some of the leading business men and railway men of this country who all state that the canal is commercially feasible. With this testimony before the House, surely the

Government ought to be in a position to Tender a verdict. - They ought to be in a position to say whether or not the canal ought to he built, and whether ot not it is going to be built. Therefore, I simply rise to second the remarks of my hon. friend from Rouville and to ask the Government for a direct answer as to whether or not they are going to build the canal.

If, instead of the very eloquent words which fell from the lips of the hon. member for Rouville and of the hon. member for Wright, those gentlemen would draft a resolution on this question and bring it before the House the results might please them better.

Resolutions have been
drafted time and again and brought before the House. Last session I, myself, drafted one and presented it to the House, following out exactly the words of the present Prime Minister. The right hon. jPrime Minister speaking on the question of trade said:
Our object is to get Canadian trade in Canadian channels, and to continue as much as we can tiie policy of making that trade run east and west.
Anybody who knows anything about the canal system of Canada, knows that by the deepening of the Welland Canal trade would run north and south instead of east and west.

The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) said: 'WThy fool the people all the time'. Then he went on to say that 50 reports have already been made on the Georgian Bay canal project. I might say that every one of those reports was in possession of the late Government for many years. I just wish to point out a few of the absurdities in the speech of the hon. member for Rouville. For instance, he mentions Sir William Van Horne, the president of the Canadian Pacific railway, who said that this canal was commercially feasible. Sir William Van Horne's opinion is embodied in a report made to the late Government in 1907-a report very exhaustive, as the hon. member for Wright has justly said, and which covers the engineering end of the canal very fully. The late Government had all this material at hand from 1906 to 1911, but they did absolutely nothing. The member for Wright has said that the late Government was absolutely in favour of building this canal. I have been in this House for the last four or five years, but I never heard the late Government make any such statement. I have heard, however,
the right hon. leader of the Opposition make the statement both in this House and at North Bay that he, personally, was in favour of the Georgian Bay canal; but during the time I have had the honour of being a member of this House, I never heard the Government commit themselves as a Government to that project. The late Hon. Mr. Tarte was very strongly in favour of building this canal, and I have also heard the ex-Mininster of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) state on several occasions that he was in favour of this project. I heard him make that statement at a by election at South Renfrew where, I think, it was one of the leading planks in his platform. I think the Government is perfectly justified m appointing this commission, although I am one of those members of this House who are first, last and all the time in favour of the completion of this work. We have had cases in point to justify the appointment of this commission-for instance, the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, a work entailing the expenditure of many millions of dollars. I do not want to state the figures as hon. gentlemen apposite might dispute them, but at any rate the figures contemplated in 1904 are not the figures given to the public to-day. This was the direct result of the fact that the Government entered into this work without knowing what they were stepping into, and I think the present Government were justified in appointing . this commission. I believe personally that the commission will report in favour of the building of the canal, and I think that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), who is not present to-day, was amply justified in saying that there was nothing to hinder this commission, if their report should be delayed for any reason, going on and reporting upon either or both ends of the canal; that is, they might build the canal from Montreal to Ottawa or Pembroke and the other end of it at the French river. It must appeal to any ordinary man who has gone over the ground as being a feasible project. I think the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) was ill-advised when he made the statement that this Government had done nothing to forward this canal, or to iofer that the late Government with all these fifty reports, as he said, on their hands, had done anything more during their sixteen years of office than this Government had done during the last one or two.

My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) seemed to

get a little bit annoyed because the Georgian Bay canal was mentioned. You cannot disassociate the two schemes in the minds of some people. There is a class of people who favour one and think that in favouring the one they must look with disfavour upon the other. I do not belong to that class, but still, in discussing the Georgian Bay canal, it is perfectly proper to discuss the Welland canal in connection with it, or vice versa. Although the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) is not in his seat and this Georgian Bay canal is in his department, the Government could not but expect that when they asked this House to discuss an appropriation for the Welland canal, the Georgian Bay canal scheme would be discussed at the same time. If the Government is not prepared to give us any information on the Georgian Bay canal that is not our fault. We must exercise our right and discuss it along with the Welland canal. My hon. friend who just sat down (Mr. Arthurs), intimated that the late Government had never been committed to the Georgian Bay canal scheme. Being a member of that Government, I think I am, in a position to say that the hon. gentleman is in error in that statement. If the Prime Minister himself be committed to the scheme, and publicly says so, if the Minister of Railways and Canals be committed to the scheme, part of which is in his department, and if the Minister of Public Works also is committed to it, that pretty nearly commits the Government, I should imagine. I see that I was criticised by the senior Conservative organ of Ottawa because I did not object to the expenditure on the Welland canal. ion that the enlarging of the Welland canal, or the building of a new Welland canal, would tend to send our traffic to the United States as has been suggested. I do not believe that. I have as a private member of this House, discussed this great question of the traffic between the East and the West between the Great Lakes and the city of Montreal and Europe. We have undoubtedly a good deal to contend against. In the first place, we have to fight the companies which make New York, Boston and Portland their ports on account of our. insurance 'rates in the St. Lawrence. I am of the opinion that the insurance companies are too severe on our Canadian route and that we ought to have better rates. I think the Government ought to wake up and establish, or have established, some new system of insurance by which these Canadian ports would not be treated as they have been treated by these companies in insurance matters. A great many millions of dollars have been expended on the St. Lawrence route from Montreal, to Quebec and my belief is that that route is a good deal safer route than the insurance companies would have us believe. Millions more would have to be expended upon it.
Then we have our St. Lawrence canals. In discussing the question of freight rates from the Great Lakes east to Montreal one or two of the leading authorities upon this question have placed their views before me on different occasions and they have contended that the freight rates at present existing could be materially decreased by the enlargement of the Welland canal, or the building of a new Welland canal, deepening the channel in some places down as far as Kingston, Brockville and Prescott, and by having, as at present, canals only fourteen feet in depth from there to Montreal. They argue, fjom their standpoint as transportation men, that the grain can be taken from any of these three ports at the end of lake navigation down to Montreal and be there reloaded more cheaply than it could be carried by the deepening of the canals and attempting to bring larger vessels up through them.
I am giving these views for what they are worth; I am not practical in this respect, but these men have practical experience, and they figured out the different rates from the different points. I put this question to them time and again: Will it tend to divert our traffic to the American ports, after the grain comes down through the Welland canal? and these men were unanimously of the opinion that.
such would not be the case, and that the rates which would be available by this Canadian route could not possibly be met by any project that the United States could undertake, for the carrying of traffic from the Lake ports, or the St. Lawrence, to New York, Boston or Portland. It will be 12 feet, while our canals are 14 feet.

Yes. One of the engineers informed me that they hoped to get 14 feet on the Erie, but so far as I have been able to see from their plans they only provide for 12 feet. They never can carry the grain a longer haul through a 12-foot canal, cheaper than we can carry it by a 14-foot canal from Prescott down; and, when they come to carry it by rail, it will be still more costly. Of course, the harbour of Montreal has got to be more thoroughly equipped for the accommodation of this traffic than it is at present. Great improvement has been made, but the carriers complain that even now they cannot get rid of their cargoes with sufficient speed so as to make good time in getting back for. other cargoes. There must be extension of the facilities at the port of Montreal. Money must be expended in making the St. Lawrence channel, east of Montreal, more safe than it is .at present. With the reduction of insurance rates which we should have on our ocean traffic, and the enlargement of the Welland canal, we will be in a position to compete all the better with the American routes for the traffic from West to East, for some years. This, of course, is only for immediate requirements. I believe, if we look at the vast amount of products which we may expect in the West, and the traffic that consequently must come from West to East and the return traffic from East to West, that in a few years, even with the Welland canal deepened and with these improvements which I have outlined carried out, we will not have sufficient water carriage for the traffic we may expect in this Dominion, and so it will be necessary to have another outlet. My own personal v'ew is, and I think it is the view of the

late Government, that that other outlet should be the Georgian Bay canal. While we are getting ready to go on with that great project, we should not hesitate to deepen the Welland canal as rapidly as possible, improve Montreal harbour and equip it with the most modern facilities, make the channel east of Montreal as perfect as we can, get cheaper insurance rates, and then proceed with that other great scheme of transportation, which will give us the benefit of further water carriage. We need the Welland canal now, and we ought to start with the Georgian Bay canal as soon as possible.

Before the House rose at six o'clock, the Georgian Bay canal was discussed by the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). A more mature deliberation upon the conditions in general of transportation at even this late date will convince people that canals as through routes are like burrowing in the earth-they have long since passed their useful stage. It is a well known fact that a very easy and safe means of transportation for enormous quantities of freight is by dirigible balloons under the control of a monoplane, or, if necessary, of a hydroplane, or, if preferred, of a biplane. A thousand tons of wheat can be trailed along at a low altitude for an enormous distance at a very high rate of speed and at a very low cost. I am fully persuaded that the people who are arguing in favour of the Georgian Bay canal are animated solely by a desire for the general benefit of Canada. .Therefore if we find that the people of the extreme West do not want it, that the people of the middle West do not want it, and that the people of the Maritime provinces do not want it-
Who said so?
I am saying so. You can say the opposite afterwards.
You cannot speak for the Maritime provinces.

I am judging by
opinions that have been expressed at different times.
You are wrong.
Leave out the Maritime provinces.
I make the assertion that the people of the Maritime provinces do not want the Georgian Bay canal.
Prove it.

I am not called upon to prove it, and it is not susceptible of proof. The contrary, moreover, is not susceptible of proof. I am merely retailing opinions which I have heard expressed. My friends may rest assured, however, that I do not attach undue weight to them, coming as they do from the Maritime provinces.
The people of the middle West have frequently said so-so I have heard and so I have read-that so far as the Georgian Bay canal is Concerned, it is of no use to them whatever. The remedy for the ills of the West is said to be free wheat, because it is to the south of us that the export of the cereals of the West should be made, they say. In that event the Georgian Bay canal will be of no use for through traffic to the West. The local traffic is not worth considering; the Georgian Bay canal would not be built merely for local traffic.
With this brief introduction, I wish to state that I know of a company forming which will undertake to transport all the food products of the West from Winnipeg to Quebec at a very much less rate than can be dreamt of by any other means, viz., the dirigible balloon, otherwise known as the airship. Hon. gentlemen, who scout and laugh at everything they hear as the Opposition are now doing, remind me of Noah, who told the people to come in out of the wet and they would not do so. I liken myself to Noah. I am perfectly serious in regard to this matter, however. I know quite well that some hon. gentlemen opposite, especially from Montreal, will scout any theory that will in any way interfere with Montreal and with their pet scheme. The Georgian Bay canal is to cost in the neighbourhood of two, three, or four hundred million dollars. For I-200th part of the sum it will take to build that canal, which will be locked up for eight months of the year and will have a repair bill which will frighten the people of this country, we are prepared to establish a line of air transportation which will carry both ways immense cargoes at a very rapid rate. These dirigible balloons can turn aside in different direction, so that there is no necessity f-or disputes about high or low grades or whether we are to have permanent ways or

trestles. These balloons, moreover, have proved themselves capable of sailing against a sixty-mile gale. It is a strange thing that these so-called peaceful men of the Opposition are willing to hand over these modern means of transportation to the devotees of war. It does not concern them that 'peace hath her victories no less renowned than war.' It does not seem to concern them that they might apply these dirigibles to the purpose of transportation for the relief of the fanner in whom they pretend to take so much interest.
There has been discovered lately a gas with one-tenth of the density of hydrogen, which has been the gas used for expanding balloons in the past. This gas can be produced very cheaply, and consequently the expense incident to a line of transportation such as I have outlined is very small. The envelope for the dirigible balloon need not b,e of fine silk, as it used to be, but can be constructed .of cheaper material; and I venture to say that in twenty-five years from now every enterprising man will have an airship or a monoplane of his own. The land is obstructed in every way, and the sea, which is the next best thing, is obstructed by rocks, icebergs, and so on. The air is really the only element that is not obstructed; and it has been finally settled between tho.se who contend for the heavier than air machine .and those who contend for the lighter than air machine that both serve their purpose, the lighter than air being for freight and the heavier for speed and direction. '
With both combined, the purposes of both are well served. You can easily imagine, Mr. Chairman, one of those great dirigible balloons-they may even be constructed 1,000 feet long-settling over a modern goods train, or its equivalent, filled with grain or whatever it may be. There is linked to it the extra chemical advantage-or aerial lightness is given to it-it is got under way by a motor, and off it glides into the air moving easily from one part to another, it might go in whatever direction wished. That seems to appeal to members of the Maritime provinces, No doubt the one from Halifax would avoid St. John, and vice versa-I may get their support on that ground. However, I wish in all earnestness to bring this matter to the attention of the Government. We are desirous of having them consider the feasibility of the project which I am now outlining, and in a short time we intend to bring it to their attention in a thoroughly practical manner. As I said, it is not necessary, especially in an intelli-188
gent House like this, to discuss the feasibi-. lity of the project because everybody knows it is feasible. A few years ago people scoffed at the telephone and wireless telephony and had no idea that wireless telegraphy was possible. Telegraphy, itself, was considered impossible until the Hertzian waves were discovered, but surely in these days no man, unless he belongs to the Opposition in this House, will say that anything is an impossibility. I admit that gentlemen on the Opposition side scoff at anything that is new-they are inclined to -scoff at anything also that is true, but I wish emphatically to call the attention of the Government to this matter with a thoroughly practical purpose in view; with the view of gaining the attention of advocates of such a scheme as the Georgian Bay canal, who will probably turn back from that project for the general benefit of Canada now that they see something much less expensive and much more serviceable. It reminds me of the story of Theseus of ancient Greece. That heroic gentleman, as no doubt Mr. Chairman you are aware, found that the bed provided by his host was too small for his gigantic frame.
