If the grain went from Ogdensburg it would have to go 400 miles to New York, and counting 1,000 bushels to .a car, at one and a quarter cents a bushel, that would be only twelve and a half dollars for that car for 400 miles. In addition you would have to pay elevatoT charges, whereas, by send-

ing it to Montreal by barge, the elevator charges would be included. If that grain came to the Welland canal and was taken to Oswego, it would have to be put in small barges and travel 400 miles by the Erie canal and the Hudson river to New York. They could not possibly carry it for so low a rate as the rate from Prescott or Kingston to Montreal. Even if the present canal were deepened, you would still have to deepen the water stretches on lake St. Louis and lake St. Francis, and that would be enormously expensive. A system of dams would keep the levels up and you could have any depth of water you needed. I think the hon. member (Mr. Graham) will agree with me that if it were not for the dam stopping the boats, it would almost pay at the present time to put a dam across the Galops rapids. That, I understand, would not be a difficult engineering feat, and because of that dam holding the water back, instead of letting it run through the rapids, the large amount now expended annually for dredging the different channels would be saved.

I am astonished and scandalized to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) advancing the idea of damming the St. Lawrence. I have heard him
9 p.m. speak, when he was in opposition, in tones of despair at the [DOT]very possibility that there might be such a scheme carried out by the then Liberal Government. For weeks and for months, day in and day out, he watched the Government for fear they would assent to the very proposition which he now favours. I was impressed by his argument in those days, and the Government would not agree to the damming of the St. Lawrence, and I hope that this Government will not agree to it either. All the reasons which he gave against damming the St. Lawrence at that time, are as true now as then; the beauty of the St. Lawrence would be marred now just as then, if a dam were erected. Moreover, there is no necessity for damming the St. Lawrence now, if the object be to keep the freight from being diverted to the New York route, because the New York route cannot compete with the St. Lawrence route. For my part, like my hon. friend (Mr. Graham), I believe we need the Georgian Bay canal, but we need the Welland canal just as much. I have the greatest hope in the Welland canal, because by it you can avail of water navigation from Port Arthur to Kingston. At present, these large beats which carry a quarter of a million bushels of grain, come to the end of the Welland canal, and have

to discharge cargo, but when we have this new Welland canal, one of these big vessels will leave Port Arthur and go to Kingston, and then her cargo can be transferred to river barges, for destination at Montreal. There is cheap freight from Kingston to Montreal, and neither Buffalo nor Oswego can compete with that route. That is the justification for the Welland canal, and the sooner it is built the better.

One would
imagine from this discussion that the port of Montreal was open throughout the winter months, and that there would be a continuous procession of grain vessels from the head of the lakes to Prescott or Kingston, whence their cargoes would be forwarded to Montreal. It is wonderful to hear the guessing competitions that are ind 'lged in in this House, about the results of this undertaking. I want to point out that the majority of the vessel-men in Canada are frightened at the deepening of the Welland canal. The port of Montreal is invariably closed on the 20th of November, and the rush of grain from the Northwest comes after that date.
I have lived in the town of Midland for thirty years, and through Midland an enormous lot of grain comes every year; so that I know whereof I speak. Hon. gentlemen no doubt know that even up to the 15th of December, when the port of Montreal has long since been closed, there is a considerable quantity of grain coming out of Port Arthur. The idea of the Canadian vessel-men is that the deepening of the Welland canal, which I suppose we are bound to go on with now, is eventually going to ruin the Canadian shipping trade, in that the immense barges of the Steel Trust, which have been in commission all summer carrying ore, will proceed to Port Arthur, get their 400,000 or 500,000 bushels of grain as a cargo, pass through the deepened Welland canal, anchor at Oswego-Montreal being closed-and by cheap handling elevators the grain will be taken out of these vessels during the winter months and shipped to New York for European destination. Freighters will not be found in the summer time lying 'around Montreal looking for cargoes, because the trade there is small. On one occasion I was at a place called Point Comfort, where Hampton Roads, a well known harbour on the American side, is situated. You can see any day large British freighters lying there at anchor. Any one will tell you that they are lying there waiting for tele-

grams from New York to tell them where they can pitek up freight. In ordeT to avoid the cost of tying up at the dock3 at New York, they are lying at Hampton Roads ready to move up to New York when a cargo is in sight. There would be a system of cheap elevators at Oswego or Ogdensburg emptying the 400,000 or 500,000 bushel freighters -and loading the grain in the oars to -be taken- to New York.
One of the -best freights for vessels on the upper l-akes is the first cargoes of -coal that go np in the spring of the year. After these vessels have dispensed with their cargoes of grain in the fail, they -will be filled with coal and will toe the first vessels to go up the lake in the spring. A year or two ago a gentleman was -advertised to s-peak in Berlin, from which place.-most of this agitation has sprung in regard to the deepening of the Welland canal, although they are as much interested in the deepening of that canal as a -man in Timbuctoo would be. This gentleman -said that it was necessary for the welfare of Canada that the Welland c-anal should toe deepened. His initials -and his name are the same as those of the general manager of one of the biggest freighting companies in Canada. At -breakfast in the hotel I had read the speech of this gentleman. I met the vessel man on the street and said, ' Are you in favour of the Welland canal?1 He said, 'You are the second man that has met me on King street that has -asked mo that question. No, I am not the gentleman who made the speech. Do you think that I as a -ship owner would ibe so crazy as to advocate the deepening of the Welland canal?' It is, however, going to be done. We are all in -a guessing competition now, but at Oswego and Ogdensburg the matter ha-s gone -beyond the guessing staige. The people -are getting prepared for the-, stern reality, -and real estate- has increased in those- places -from twenty-five to thirty per cent by reason of the fa-ct that the Canadian Government is to deepen the Welland canal and thus giv-e them access to the lakes.

Lake Ontario will -be
open and the boats will toe -aJble to come down the lakes.
From Oswego?

By a -system of cheap elevators that will handle the grain out of
these -huge vessels, -carrying 400,000 or 500,000 bushels. It is nothing unusual to see on the upper lakes vessels capable o-f carrying 500,000 bushels. These elevators will put the grain into the cars which will take it to New York, w-hi-ch is open all the year around.

Is Kingston closed any more than Oswego? Do you forget my little
village?

In the meantime it is the duty of the Government to do everything possible to improve the elevator facillities at Montreal so as to get as much grain down there as possible in the fall, and then by a system of iice-toreakers to endeavour to keep the harbour of Montreal open later than the 20th or 23rd of November.

I agree with the hon.
member in so far as the advisability of providing the very best elevator localities -at Montreal for (handling grain is concerned, but I -c-annot agree with his conclusions in regard to the probable movement o-f the grain, if the Welland canal is deepened and enlarged, as we propose doing. I am not prepared to say just what the difference is, but I do not think there is very much difference between the distance from Kingston via Montreal to St. John and the distance from Oswego to New York.
It is shorter to St. John.

So far as railway freight rates are concerned, the grain could be shipped from Kingston or Prescott just as cheaply over Canadian railways to the Canadian port of St. John as over American railways to the port of New York. If that is true, then surely we would all prefer to see that grain passing from the port of Kingston or Prescott over Canadian railways to St. John, where this Government and previous Governments have spent large sums of money, than to see it passing through the United States to the port of New York. I think I can take that for granted. I could not help wondering if my hon. friend would not have the town of Midland in his eye when he was discussing the deepening of the Welland canal.
I think I have heard the hon. gentleman advocate a grain railway from Midland to Montreal.
They have two of them now.

I think the hon. gentleman was advocating another; I will not be sure. If the Welland canal is not deepened, the effect would be, I suppose, to turn the grain to Midland to be shipped by rail to Montreal. I cannot blame my hon. friend for desiring to see the grain go through his own town. That is a local patriotism of which we all should have more or less. I should like to see the Welland canal deepened and the grain brought down by vessel-
To help Kingston.

Yes, and incidentally to help the old historic county of Frontenac. 
The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) Quoted from the Grain Markets report. I think that report speaks very favourably of the deepening of the Welland canal and carrying the grain down to the port of Kingston. I read the report carefully, and I do not recollect that any fear is expressed of the grain going to Oswego and down through the United States. I think the deepening of the Welland canal is one of the best movements which has been made; and I do not say that merely because I believe it will assist in developing Kingston, but it seems to me the reasonable and logical thing to do. Nature has provided a waterway in our splendid chain of lakes. If the grain is carried without breaking bulk from Fort William to Kingston or Prescott it can be transferred to very cheaply constructed grain barges to be taken to Montreal. I notice that is one of the things that cheapens the handling of grain in the Erie canal. The grain goes into barges which are practically boxes. They are not made to resist a heavy-sea, nor is it necessary they should be so made. In the same way, when the large steamer comes to Kingston or Prescott, the grain will be unloaded into barges which will praetially be floating bins which can make the trip to Montreal, though they could not stand the seas on the lakes. And as they are cheaply constructed, they will help to cheapen the freight rates. I think the movement is one in the right direction.

It is so seldom I have the good fortune to agree with my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) that I am glad to take the opportunity to declare such an agreement when it occurs. But even on this occasion, I am afraid, I cannot go with him .all the way. I do believe, as he does, that the best and most profitable route for grain from the West is via large freighters to Midland and then by rail to Montreal.
Mr. W. H. S-HARPE: How about the Hudson Bay railway ?

If the hon. member will have patience, we will come to that. It seems to me that the freighter of maximum [DOT]capacity carrying grain to Midland, with quick loading, quick discharge and quick return, could handle more grain in a *specified time than a freighter of less size making a longer trip. And, as it is important to get as much as possible of the grain out in the fall, I think this is the route that offers the best advantage. But

because that is a good route, it does not follow there should not be others. I cannot follow my hon. friend when he, if I understood him aright, protested against [DOT]the improvement of the Welland canal, for the reason, as he alleges, that it will fosteT the transport of grain to New York. Under present conditions altogether too large a proportion of our western grain goes to New York, although the Welland canal has .not been improved. I cannot think, as the hon. gentleman seems to do, that there is some deep-laid plot or conjunction of effort, as between the Government of the United States and the Government of Canada in the building of the Welland canal, against the well-being of the port of Midland. For I would remind him that, not the Government of the United States, it is true, but the government of the state of New York, is spending $200,000,000 in improving the Erie canal, the result of which expenditure would not have a bearing at all on the transport of grain via the Welland canal. That is, if the Welland *canal is improved, the grain goes to Kingston or Oswego, and merely renders the Erie canal useless to that extent. Now, [DOT]my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe) wants to know about the Hudson Bay railway. With the production we have in the West, and with the production we ought to have in the near future, we want, and [DOT]absolutely need, the advantage of all the outlets that can be secured. It was many [DOT]years ago that a great transportation authority declared that what Canada needed was the enlargement of the spout- of the means of getting the grain out in the shortest time. So, while we approve of the improvement of the Welland canal, we approve .also of the Hudson Bay railway, and also of means of access to the milling .centres south of the line. We approve of the Transcontinental giving us a route to the Pacific, and also a winter haul to ,the Atlantic. I am unable to put the case just as I would like, but if we are to have the development that we hope to have, we need all these different outlets, and unless we have all these different outlets we cannot achieve that development that we hope to have. We need them all, and we need them under the most favourable circumstances.

With reference to the grain going via Ogdensburg, the Welland canal will benefit trade between the East and the West during the whole season of navigation. The only time when there
might be some disadvantage would be in the fall of the year, when the vessels anchor at Ogdensburg. That was the point taken by the hon. member for Simcoe. I think he is in error in saying that the grain will be unloaded there; it will be unloaded, as the hon. member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) has stated, at Kingston or Prescott.
Prescott in preference.

But then it should be the duty, and no doubt will be the duty, of the Government to see that the grain is not diverted to Portland or other United States ports. The distance from Kingston or Prescott to St. John and Halifax is practically the same as to New York, and surely the Government of Canada, with two roads running to St. John and Halifax, the Intercolonial railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific, can keep the rates as low as those from an American port to New York, so we should have it in our own. control. The difficulty has been that we have not had the facilities at St. John or Halifax to handle the grain during the winter months, and it has gone to Portland and New York. At Halifax there is one small elevator. Last winter a few large steamers came there, and over two million bushels of grain were handled there in the few winter months. But facilities were improved last year, and they have been able to handle more grain. I am satisfied that the amount handled at St. John has increased also. The Canadian Pacific railway are building a large elevator there, and have no doubt that all these elevators will be kept busy. It is absolutely necessary that we should, at the earliest possible moment, improve the facilities at Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax, so that we may handle the products of the West and of Ontario and Quebec through Canadian ports. When we are in a position to do that the grain will go by our ports. It is not likely that large vessels will go to Oswego. They can make three trips to Midland to one to Oswego, and make a great deal more money. Grain going by Oswego would have to pass through 340 miles of canal with 30 locks to New York, as against 175 miles to Montreal from Kingston or 123 miles from Prescott. The advantage of these large vessels coming down to Kingston is that they would only have thirty miles of canal from the time between Port Arthur and Kingston.

What does the minister consider the stretch from Sarnia

down to Detroit? Is that not canal? They slow down all the way.
No, they do not. They slow down part of the way through 1'ake St. Clair, and that is all.

The river may be not as deep in some places, and. they may have to slow down a little; but I have never recognized that as part of the canal. Look what has happened since the elevator was built at Port Colborne. Prior to that all the vessels that went through the Welland canal went to Port Arthur and got their cargo to return to Montreal. The late Mr. Tarte as Minister of Public Works devised the scheme of building an elevator at Port Colborne to be used until the canal could !be enlarged. Last year that one million bushel elevator handled over twenty million bushels of grain. Large freighters 'bring it to Port Colborne and the other small Welland canal boats have been running from Port Colborne lo Montreal. My opinion is that as soon as the Welland canal is enlarged the large boats can go down to Kingston and there transfer to the same boats that now go to Port Colborne or else large barges will be built for the purpose. Personally I have not any fear, Ido not think any man who understands the situation has any fear, of either Buffalo, Oswego or Ugdensburg or any place affecting the grain going to Montreal when the Welland canal is built. As to Ogdemsbuig, it is many more miles from Ogdensburg to New York than from Buffalo to New York. It ;s not likely that a vessel will come all the way down through the Welland canal, across lake Ontario, down the St. Lawrence to stop at Ogdensburg in order to ship the grain to New York.
By rail.

Yes, by rail. It is absurd to make any such statement. There may be a little more grain come down to Ogdensburg for their own use in the eastern states adjacent to Ogdensburg as it is a distributing point for grain for use in small mills in that section just as Kingston and Prescott are for places back from the river.

I would like to have a word to say in regard to this question of transportation. I am inclined ,to think that many hon. gentlemen who 'have spoken on the matter really know very little about it. The hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals-probably he may be Minister of Railways later on, but we hope not, because we want to see the present minister continue in that office-must remember that vessels

carrying grain from Port Arthur, or Duluth, to Buffalo or Port Colborne, do not make their money in carrying that grain, but in carrying coal back to western points. It has been stated that the enlarging of the Welland carnal will mean that American boats will go to Ogdensburg. No doubt they will, but they will have to go back through the Welland canal, and take their load of coal for the West just the same as the Canadian boats; so there is no reason why the Welland canal should be any more advantageous to American than to Canadian shipping. For myself, the Welland canal construction is beneficial. I would like to see the St. Lawrence route deepened and, with due deference to other opinions, I would like to see dams put in at every rapid on the St. Lawrence, and the river made navigable. That is what will happen in the future, and electric power development will pay the whole cost of construction. My own idea is that the scenic problem is practically obliterated, or will be in a few years. So far as the Georgian Bay canal is concerned, I h-ave never taken part in the many discussions which have taken place hitherto, because I rather thought that if I discussed the Georgian Bay canal hon. members would say: You are absolutely in favour of the Welland canal and consequently opposed to the Georgian Bay canal. And each year is as long or as short as another, and there are 365 days in a year now, just as there were then, and my hon. friend from North Renfrew will not be able to escape responsibility by any suggestion of that kind.

We will help the

Why, the Hudson
Bay railway was provided for and the contract let by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) before the Liberal Government went out of power. I believe that the voyageurs of centuries ago found the true water passage from the Lower St. Lawrence to the West when they went up the Ottawa river and followed the line of What is now called the Georgian Bay route, and that in this twentieth century that water route should be improved, so as to meet the modem requirements 'and conditions of traffic by water. I agree with my hon. friend from North Renfrew (Mr. White) as to the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, but I do ask him to be big enough to realize that the men whom he supports will never move if he continues to make such speeches as he has made to-night. They will sit in placid contentment and say: as long as the repre-

sentatives of the people most interested in that project Tyill defend us when iwe do nothing, we will continue our policy of doing nothing on this, as on every other question. I believe that the Georgian Bay route should be the great national waterway of this-country, and that the conditions are such that this Government, having found when they came into power an overflowing treasury-which they have been dissipating day after day to political favourites in [DOT]regard to every petty project presented to -them-ought, at once, to have proceeded to move in the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. They at least might commence to deal with some item of their programme. The people interested in this project will hold these men to account for their inactivity, and their inability to conceive or construct anything. The defence put forward by my bon. friend from North Renfrew and others like him, for the inaction of the Government in this matter, wall be easily understood by the plain people of this country.

I would not wish to have any misunderstanding in regard to the position of the late Government towards this project, or my own. As a representative of the West, I have always objected to those who favoured the construction of the Georgian Bay canal putting it forward as a project in the interest of the West. The West has always been and will always be prepared- to pay its share for the development of this country, either in the East or in the West. If it should seem good to the people of Canada to build the Georgian Bay canal, I am satisfied that our western people will be ready to bear their share of the burden of cost. For my own part, I have always held the view that the construction of the Georgian Bay canal was not an essential to the development of the West, any more than the construction of any other single means of ingress or egress for the products of the West. If we have a transcontinental railway carrying freight winter and summer; if we have the lake routes as we have them now; if we .have the improved Welland canal; if we have the Hudson Bay railway; if we have access to the markets of the world by way of the Pacific; if we have access to the American milling centres by the American railways, we are not in a position of such urgent need that we should demand that the people of Canada pay $100,000,000 or $200,000,000 towards the construction of still another means of access which will

only be of use during a part of the year. I hope I have made my position clear. We do not object to the building of the Georgian Bay canal; we do not object to the paying of our share of it, but we object to being saddled with the responsibility for its construction as being a necessity for western development. As a national undertaking, for the benefit of the nation, if the nation at large thinks well, we are quite willing to pay our share;, but for my part-and I think there are other gentlemen from the West who will take exactly the same stand-we certainly object to western Canada being saddled with the responsibility for that vast expenditure as being for the benefit primarily of the West.

I do not think the hon. gentleman should look at the matter from that point of view. It is what is going to be of advantage not only to the West but to all Canada. I think my hon. friend from Edmonton is taking a very sectional view of the matter.

The engineers of the Department of Railways and Canals.

Of both Governments.

figure on the rate they can get from Fort William to Rotterdam or to Liverpool, iwherever the wheat is going. While a man in Winnipeg has been negotiating sales of wheat through a New York house, perhaps [DOT]a man in Chicago has been selling corn through a Montreal house. I venture to say that our canals, since they have been constructed, have carried as much United States grain as Canadian grain. It is nonsense for us to discuss the question as .to whether grain will go through United .States ports or through Canadian ports; it is all an interchange of business. A man who owns corn will use the Canadian route because it is a northerly and therefor a cooler route, and his. com transhipped at Kingston or Prescott will be shipped to Montreal and will go through in better condition. If wheat is in good condition, it can be routed cheaper by New York; and it will go through that port whether you build the Georgian Bay canal or the Welland canal.
There is also the question of insurance. At certain seasons of the year there is a discrimination of half a cent to three-quarters of a cent a bushel in the insurance rate between the Montreal route and the New York route. Shortly after this Government came into power, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who recognized that discrimination, went to Montreal, met the Board of Trade, and admitted that that w.as the real issue. He endeavoured to remedy the matter.
From that day to this, so far as I know, there has not been one sixteenth change in the insurance rates downwards, but the rate did go up last fall. Our friends opposite had better get to work and try to do something towards carrying out their promises in regard to insurance rates.

Let me offer a word of paternal advice to the minister. Do not boast unduly that a contract is made at a lower figure than the estimate. Better to boast of that after it is all over. The esti-

mate of the engineer is an approximate estimate only and allows all the tenderers to base their figures on the same information. But it does not necessarily cover all the work to be done; the quantities may be different from those estimated. The probabilities are the work will cost eventually-without any dishonesty, but under the system-a good deal more than the original estimate, because the quantities will vary.
A great deal of dispute arises in connection with these larger contracts. An engineer will estimate so much solid rock and so much excavation of a certain kind of clay and so much loose rock and so on. These are estimates, and when the work comes to be done contractors and engineers may find a great deal more solid rock than they anticipated, even by boring. The final cost of the work will vaTy a great deal although the contractors will have tendered on the same basis. I would advise my hon. friend, who has rather gloried that the tenders are less than the estimates, that the time to glory is when the contract is through and the bills are paid, not when the contracts are let.

Is that the time that Mr. Weller was sent down there?

Yes, Mr. Butler was ill, and I wired for Mr. Weller to come and take charge of the work. A portion of the bridge of the company had been carried away and another portion had not been carried away. In order to expedite the restoration of navigation it was necessary to remove a certain portion of the bridge that still stood. My recollection is that the manager of the road was there with Mr. Weller, myself and the superintendent. We had no time to discuss ways and means; this thing had to be done quickly. After consultation with Mr. Weller, I said to the company: Do whatever Mr. Weller asks you to do to get your property out of the way so that we can get this work done quickly. I had it in. my mind that the Government would pay" for any work ordered in that way. Later a claim was made against the-Government for damages to the bridge on account of the break and a certain amount was asked for this work. I i efueed absolutely to pay the account because there was a claim for damages included in it. I said that the company in building the bridge across the canal took the risk of any breaks that might occur. I do think that they should not be paid one cent for damages, but I think it would be fair to pay them a reasonable amount for the work I ordered them to do.

I received a letter a few days ago from this company asking me to pay an account. I cannot recall whether there was anything in it for damages or not but they stated in this letter that the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) had been present and had ordered the work to be done. Of course, I quite understand that in a case of that kind there was nothing else to do and that the Government should pay for anything the hon. member, or the engineer, ordered done because you could not possibly wait. I asked the deputy minister to write to the hon. member and I said that whatever he had ordered would be paid for. Whatever arrangement the hon. member recollects having made in reference to the matter will certainly be carried out as far as I am concerned. If I find any difficulty in coming to a conclusion after going oyer the matter I shall certainly take it up with the hon. member and endeavour to come to some* arrangement that is fair and just.

The reason I did not settle the matter was that I would not consider any question of damages.

11 p.m. Mr. ROBB: I submit to the minister's spirit of fair play these circumstances. These people were given the contract at Ottawa on the 26tlh July, -and it is reasonable to think that they would h-ave a week to get to work. They had hardly been awarded the contract when the Montreal cotton mills -began to receive coal at this dock, and when the contractors started working at one place, the engineer would mo-ve them to -another place, -and then -a barge would -come in there -and they would have to be moved back again. I was in Valleyfield at the -time, and I knew all that was going ' on. It so happened that the lowest tenderers were Liberals. If they were not Liberals they were Ministerialists. The minister will know what a Ministerialist is. They formerly supported the Liberal party, and there was a row among some of tfhe Conservatives when this work was given to Cossette Brothers. Immediately delegations started foT Ottawa and petitions were sent saying that these contractors must be stopped from doing that work.
I never heard of that before.

The work was delayed; the cold weather came on in the fall, and they could not put men to work in the icy water. The contractors were prepared to go on with the work this spring, when they discovered that their opponents in Valieyfield were objecting to their doing the work. Then there -was an arrange* ment with another gentleman who had been a life-long Conservative, to transfer the contract to him, but the political friends of the minister in Valieyfield objected to that and insisted on the minister cancelling the contract, and punishing the Liberal contractors by forfeiting their deposit. That is the -history of the case. The minister knows these men were punished at the request oi his political friends at Valieyfield.

The hon. gentleman is not fair in putting it in that way. All this has occurred recently, and I do not think it came before Mr. Cochrane at all, but, so far as I am concerned, it is the first time I have heard what the politics of the contractors are. I never heard mention made of that before. No person has been up to see me from Valieyfield or from any other place to have this contract transferred from this firm to a Conservative in Valley-field, except one man, but I have never seen any petition.

What is that man's name?
Mr. REID* I think it is Boyer; but I refused to transfer it to him. I am informed by the officials that the object in getting this contract was to get a change in the contract on account of the railway the contractor was promoting in Valieyfield, or some other reason of that kind. At all events, I can assure the hon. member (Mr. Robb) that there was nothing political in the matter at all, and no suggestion of that kind was -ever made to me. This firm did not seem to take any interest in the work, and if I had not been informed by the official that there was no chance of them going ahead, I would not have agreed to the cancellation of the contract.

I can assure the minister that these contractors have already spent three or four thousand dollars on this work, which is to cost $16,000. The contractors are really in earnest and intend to do the work. As my hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) has said, it is a political quarrel, and this cancellation of the contract is an attempt to choke them
off and to confiscate the work they have done. Petitions have been signed in Valieyfield by 25 or 30 persons, and I have no doubt they have been forwarded here. The contractors were working at that contract for about two months last fall, and when they could not work in the river they were preparing material to commence the work this spring. They asked for an extension of time in good faith. I believe these contractors are the best men in Valieyfield to do that work.
If they have spent $3,000 or $4,000 on a $16,000 contract, it is surprising to me that they never made application for a progress estimate.
They were preparing the material and getting in plant, and they could not have asked for an estimate before the concrete was put in.

In every contract progress
estimates are made on the material before it is put into the work. From July up to the present time these contractors have never asked for a progress estimate and they never made any claims since we have cancelled the contract.

It is well known in
Valieyfield that they encountered so much opposition from the- engineers that they preferred to cease work and ask for an extension of the contract this year.

That may have been going
on in Valieyfield; and it may have been the impression of the contractors; but, so far as I personally am concerned, their complaint never reached me and the chief engineer states that such a complaint as the hon. member states never reached him. I can assure the hon. member that the contract was not cancelled on account of the political situation; the contract was cancelled entirely on the recommendation of the engineers that these people would not go on with the work. They did not seem to have any desire to go ahead; -and if we wanted to get the work done, the only thing to do was to cancel the contract and ask for new tenders.
Is it the policy of the department to cancel all contracts that come before it?

We certainly do not do so, as long as a contractor shows good intentions of completing his work. That has been the system with all governments.

When we award a contract and the woirk does not proceed and is not likely to proceed, then the contract is cancelled. I am satisfied that every government since Confederation have cancelled contracts during the time they were in power. It seldom occurs, but it certainly does occur.

We have just told the minister that these men were so delayed last fall that it was simply impossible for them to do the work on account of his engineers who kept them back. The men ware ready to go on with their work this spring and came to the minister asking for -an extension of the contract so that they might do so. When their contract expired on the 31st of March, they applied for an extension of time so that on the 1st of April they might commence work when the ice went out, but they were not given that extension.

So far as I understand from the officials of the department, these people never brought a dredge there at all, although a dredge was necessary for that work. They were trying to do the work with a diver. I do not remember meeting any member of this firm; but they interviewed the chief engineer a few days before the contract was cancelled, and they stated that they did not wish to go on with the work at all; all that they wanted was the return of their deposit. I acted entirely on the recommendation of the officials of the department, and no one asked me to cancel this contract because these men were not supporters of the Government. We have cancelled the contract; they have not asked for any more than their deposit back, -and that is a matter that I personally have not the power to decide. Once a deposit is made on a contract, it requires an Order in Council or a vote of the House to refund it. We would have to put it in the Estimates, and a matter of that kind would have to be considered by Council before it could be brought before the House.

The matter was handled by the engineers of the department; I acted on their recommendation, and the contract was cancelled. We cannot do anything now but have a new contract. There is the question of the deposit which will have to be taken up at some future time.

After the lengthy statement by the hon. member from Beauhar-nois (Mr. Papineau), who seems to know the situation thoroughly, I hope the minister will look into the matter; and if it is as stated, that the men were prevented by the engineers from proceeding with the work for certain reasons, I think it might well be considered a case for the return of their deposit; because deposits have been returned before when the contractors have not been at fault.

I will certainly look into the matter; and, if conditions are as the hon. member states, the contractors are certainly entitled to consideration. We do not want to take advantage of them if the fault has not been theirs.
Many affidavits can be produced in proof of what I have stated.

We had better let this item stand so that we can discuss it again.
Item stands.
Soulanges canal - rebuilding of wharfs,

Where are they building
these wharfs?

The two wharfs mentioned
were built by the Department of Public Works at the time of the construction of the canal, and they have both fallen into decay to such an extent that they have to be entirely rebuilt. These being on a canal it seems reasonable they should be under the jurisdiction of this department.
Soulanges canal-draining Clements' gully, $50,000.

This ditch which is cut
through the very soft clay to be found almost everywhere on the Soulanges canal has always given a great deal of trouble and its maintenance therefore has been exceedingly

expensive. The concrete abutments of a number of farm bridges spanning the ditch have fallen down, and it is only a question of time when the others will tumble down also. It had been intended to line the bottom and slopes of the cut with concrete slabs and to reinforce the floorings of the bridge at a cost of $40,000. But the scheme now proposed comprises the laying of 7,200 lineal feet of 44 feet reinforced concrete pipe. This will entail a somewhat larger expenditure, but when completed the cost of maintenance will be reduced to a minimum.
St. Peter's canal-Improvements, $135,000.

How much has been paid
the contractor?
About $60,000 has been paid up to the present time.
I think the tender put in by the present contractor was very much lower than the tender of the next above him.
Very much.

So much so that it would be scarcely possible for him to make a profit, assuming that the others were right. Did I understand the minister to say this afternoon that the changes proposed in the plans involved $100,000?
